lessons.title: Types and principles of positive displacement pumps
lessons.html:
How they differ from centrifugal pumps

A positive displacement (PD) pump traps a fixed volume of liquid and forces it out with each stroke or revolution. Flow depends mainly on speed, not on the pressure against it. That makes PD pumps ideal for accurate dosing, high pressures, viscous liquids and low-yield boreholes.

The most important rule: a PD pump must never run against a closed outlet. Pressure rises until a pipe, fitting or the pump itself fails. A correctly set pressure relief valve must protect the discharge.

Common types

TypePrincipleTypical farm or water use
Piston / plunger (reciprocating)Piston moves in a cylinder with inlet and outlet valvesHigh-pressure sprayers, cleaners, windmill pumps
DiaphragmFlexing diaphragm with check valves; no seals in contact with liquidChemical dosing, sprayers, fertigation metering
Progressive cavity (helical rotor)Metal rotor turns in a rubber stator, forming moving cavitiesBoreholes, solar pumping, sludge and slurry
GearMeshing gears carry liquid around the casingOils, hydraulic systems, fuel transfer
Lobe and vaneRotating lobes or sliding vanesFood, transfer pumps
Peristaltic (hose)Rollers squeeze a flexible tubeDosing chlorine and acids

Wear parts

  • Valves, valve seats and springs (piston and diaphragm)
  • Piston cups, packing or seals
  • Diaphragms
  • Stators and rotors (progressive cavity)
  • Gears, bushes and side plates
  • Hoses (peristaltic)

Abrasive water, dry running, wrong chemicals for the materials and excess pressure all shorten life.

Safety

Lock out drives, release pressure through the relief or drain, and know the liquid being pumped: chemical dosing pumps can contain concentrated acid, chlorine or fertiliser. Wear PPE as the safety data sheet requires.

lessons.title: Maintaining and repairing positive displacement pumps
lessons.html:
Routine checks

  • Pressure at the discharge and relief valve setting
  • Flow or dosing rate compared with the setting (calibration cylinder for dosing pumps)
  • Leaks at seals, diaphragms and connections
  • Noise and knocking, which can mean worn valves, air in the suction or a loose drive
  • Oil level and condition in crankcases and gearboxes
  • Belt tension, pulleys and guards

Piston pump service

  1. Isolate and depressurise.
  2. Remove valve caps; inspect valves, seats and springs for wear, cracks and debris; replace as a set.
  3. Inspect piston cups or plunger seals; replace if leaking or scored.
  4. Change crankcase oil at the interval specified.
  5. Check pulsation dampener (air chamber) charge where fitted.

Diaphragm pump service

  • Replace diaphragms at the interval specified or at the first sign of liquid in the oil or air chamber.
  • Clean and inspect check valves; crystallised chemical deposits often cause loss of dosing.
  • Flush chemical pumps with clean water before opening.

Progressive cavity pump service

  • Check output: falling flow at the same speed indicates stator wear.
  • Replace stator and, if worn, rotor; lubricate as the manufacturer instructs on assembly.
  • Check universal joints or flexible shaft, and the shaft seal or gland.
  • Fit or test dry-run protection.

Gear pump service

  • Check end clearance and bushes; worn parts reduce pressure.
  • Replace shaft seals; use the right seal material for the liquid.

Reassembly and testing

Use manufacturer's spare parts and torque values. Prime the suction, start with discharge open, set and test the relief valve, check flow or dosing rate, look for leaks and record readings.

lessons.title: Fault finding and records
lessons.html:
Fault-finding guide

SymptomPossible causesAction
No flowSuction blocked, air leak, valve stuck, empty tank, broken driveCheck suction line, strainer, tank level, valves, drive
Low flow or dosingWorn valves or seals, stator worn, speed low, air in suctionInspect wear parts; bleed air; check speed
Excess pressure, relief valve openingBlocked or closed discharge, blocked filterFind blockage; never block the relief valve
Knocking or pulsationWorn valves, low pulsation dampener charge, cavitationService valves; recharge dampener; check suction
LeakageWorn seals or diaphragm, loose fittingsReplace seals or diaphragm; tighten
OverheatingRunning dry, too high pressure, lack of lubricationStop; find cause; never run dry
Liquid in oilRuptured diaphragm or sealStop at once; replace diaphragm and oil

Planning maintenance

Use run hours and condition to plan service: dosing pumps on fertigation systems before the season starts; borehole progressive cavity pumps when flow drops; sprayer pumps after each season with a flush and storage oil if recommended. Keep common spares (valve kits, diaphragms, seals, stators) on hand for critical pumps.

Records

  • Pump make, model, serial number, liquid pumped and materials of wetted parts
  • Relief valve setting and test date
  • Calibration results for dosing pumps
  • Service dates, parts replaced, hours run and readings
  • Faults and root causes

Records help identify recurring faults, such as a stator failing because a dry-run switch is not working, so the real cause can be fixed.

Key points

  • PD pump flow depends on speed, not pressure; never run against a closed outlet.
  • A relief valve must protect the discharge and must never be blocked.
  • Valves, seals, diaphragms and stators are the main wear parts.
  • Flush chemical pumps and wear PPE before opening them.
  • Calibrate dosing pumps and keep records to find root causes.
